questions.text:
SQL allows duplicate tuples in relations, and correspondingly defines the multiplicity of tuples in the result of joins. Which one of the following queries always gives the same answer as the nested query shown below:
Select * from R where a in (select S. a from S)
questions.solution:
The IN query returns each R tuple once per its own copy in R, no matter how many matching tuples S has.

- Option 1: a plain join repeats an R tuple once for every matching S tuple [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] extra duplicates.
- Option 2: DISTINCT also removes duplicates that were genuinely in R.
- Option 3: S1 has each value of a only once, so every R tuple matches at most once [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] same result.

Answer: Select R.* from R, (select distinct a from S) as S1 where R.a = S1.a

options: Select R. * from R, S where R. a=S. a
Select distinct R. * from R,S where R. a=S. a
Select R. * from R, (select distinct a from S) as S1 where R. a=S1.a
Select R. * from R, S where R.a = S. a and is unique R

questions.text:
Consider a join (relation algebra) between relations r(R)and s(S) using the nested loop
method. There are 3 buffers each of size equal to disk block size, out of which one buffer is
reserved for intermediate results. Assuming size(r(R))[latex]\lt[/latex]size(s(S)), the join will have fewer
number of disk block accesses if
questions.solution:
With one buffer each for the outer and inner relation, block accesses = [latex]b_{outer}+b_{outer}\times b_{inner}[/latex].

The product term is the same either way, so the cost is smaller when the outer relation has fewer blocks. Since r is smaller, put r in the outer loop.

Answer: relation r(R) is in the outer loop

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: relation r(R) is in the outer loop.
relation s(S) is in the outer loop
join selection factor between r(R) and s(S) is more than 0.5.

questions.text:
Consider the following schedule S of transactions T1, T2, T3, T4:

Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Order: R2(X), W3(X), C3, W1(X), C1, W2(Y), R2(Z), C2, R4(X), R4(Y), C4.

Conflict edges: T2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]T3, T2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]T1, T3[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]T1 (on X), T1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]T4, T3[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]T4 (on X), T2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]T4 (on Y). No cycle [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] conflict serializable (T2, T3, T1, T4).

T4 reads X from T1 and Y from T2, and both commit before T4 commits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] recoverable.

Answer: S is both conflict-serializable and recoverable

questions.text:
Given an instance of the STUDENTS relation as shown below

For (StudentName, StudentAge) to be a key for this instance, the value x should NOT be equal to_______.
questions.solution:
Another row already has (Shankar, 19) (StudentID 7853).

If x = 19, row 2345 would also be (Shankar, 19), and (StudentName, StudentAge) would no longer be unique.

Answer: 19

questions.text:
The maximum number of super keys for the relation schema R (E, F, G, H) with E as the key
is __________.
questions.solution:
A super key must contain E. The other attributes F, G, H may or may not be included.

[latex]2^3=8[/latex] super keys.

Answer: 8
